prose_changes.old: After the old Aksumite kingdom faded, a dynasty called the Zagwe ruled the Ethiopian highlands from the twelfth century, and under them the Ethiopian church went on doing what it had done for eight hundred years — with one striking peculiarity of constitution: its head bishop, the abun, was not Ethiopian but a monk sent from the Coptic patriarchate in Egypt, so a wholly independent kingdom kept its senior churchman permanently on loan from another country. The dynasty's most famous achievement is the group of eleven churches cut downward out of solid rock at the town now called Lalibela, after the king who commissioned them, laid out to recall Jerusalem at a time when Jerusalem itself had become unreachable. In 1270 the Zagwe were displaced by Yekuno Amlak, whose line claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba — a claim set out in the Kebra Nagast, compiled in the generations after the takeover and used to justify Ethiopian kingship for the next seven centuries.
prose_changes.new: After the old kingdom of Aksum faded, a new line of kings, the Zagwe, ruled the Ethiopian highlands from the twelfth century. Under them the church went on as it had for eight hundred years, with one odd feature. Its head bishop, the abun, was not Ethiopian but a monk sent from the Coptic patriarch in Egypt. So a free kingdom kept its senior churchman on loan from another land. The Zagwe are best known for eleven churches cut downward into solid rock. They stand at the town now called Lalibela, after the king who had them made. Several bear the names of holy places, such as Golgotha and Bethlehem. A Portuguese visitor in the 1520s was shown a tomb there said to copy Christ's tomb in Jerusalem. In 1270 Yekuno Amlak pushed the Zagwe aside, and his line claimed descent from Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. The Kebra Nagast, put together in the generations after he took power, set out that claim. Ethiopian kings leaned on it for the next seven centuries.
prose_changes.reason: Two sentences qualified: 'laid out to recall Jerusalem at a time when Jerusalem itself had become unreachable' has no vendored support, and Ethiopian monks are not shown cut off from Jerusalem. Alvares (1520s, lines 6076-6079, 6120-6121) gives church names Golgotha and Bethlehem and a tomb 'after the manner of the sepulchre of Christ in Jerusalem'; the sentence now says only that. Paragraph re-cut for readability; every other fact kept. FRE 11.6 / FK 25.1 before.

prose_changes.old: The Coptic Orthodox Church is very much alive — the largest Christian community in the Middle East — and runs unbroken through this period. The work done here lasted: the al-Assal brothers' canonical collections stayed authoritative in the Coptic church for centuries and were carried south into Ethiopia, where the Fetha Nagast, the law book of the Ethiopian state into the twentieth century, derives from al-Safi's canons. Their grammars and dictionaries are much of the reason the Coptic language is recoverable at all today. The Hanging Church in Old Cairo, which served as the patriarch's seat for most of this period, is still standing and still in use.
prose_changes.new: The Coptic Orthodox Church is very much alive. It is the largest Christian community in the Middle East, and it runs unbroken through this period. Some of the work done here may have travelled south. The Fetha Nagast, the law book of the Ethiopian state into the twentieth century, is usually traced to al-Safi's canons, but we have not yet checked this against the Ethiopian text. The brothers' grammars and dictionaries are much of the reason the Coptic language is recoverable at all today. The Hanging Church in Old Cairo, the patriarch's seat for most of this period, still stands and is still in use.

prose_changes.old: The Church of the East still exists, but this was its last period of long reach. The Mongol elite in Persia turned to Islam within a generation of Yahballaha's death, and the fourteenth century brought the catastrophe — Timur's campaigns above all — that reduced a church once stretching from Cyprus to China to a mountain remnant in Hakkari. Its traces are now mostly archaeological: Syriac gravestones scattered across Central Asia, Christian tomb carvings in the Chinese port cities. The account of Bar Sauma's embassy remains the single most remarkable thing this period produced.
prose_changes.new: The Church of the East still exists, but this was its last age of long reach. Ghazan, the Mongol ruler of Persia, had turned to Islam in 1295, while Yahballaha was still head of the church. Then the fourteenth century brought disaster, above all Timur's wars. A church that once ran from Cyprus to China shrank to a mountain remnant in Hakkari. Its traces now are mostly in the ground: Syriac gravestones across Central Asia, and Christian tomb carvings in China's port cities. The account of Bar Sauma's embassy is still the most remarkable thing this age produced.
prose_changes.reason: Factual fix: the Mongol ruler of Persia turned to Islam in 1295, during Yahballaha's lifetime, not 'within a generation of [his] death'. The History records the 1295 turn against the church and the 'Muslim Mongols' (Budge lines 8449-8460, 8768); Chabot's note says Nauruz persuaded Ghazan to embrace Islam (Chabot 1895, line 7040). Re-cut for readability. FRE 41.9 / FK 13.1 before.

prose_changes.old: The Syriac Orthodox Church continues today, with its patriarchate now in Damascus and a large diaspora. The books written here never went out of use. Michael's chronicle and Bar Hebraeus's histories are still primary sources for anyone working on the medieval Middle East, and Bar Hebraeus's canonical and grammatical works stayed standard in the Syriac churches for centuries. This period is generally reckoned the last great flowering of Syriac letters before the long contraction that followed, which is why later Syriac writers kept looking back to it.
prose_changes.new: The Syriac Orthodox Church lives on today, with its patriarch now in Damascus and a large community abroad. The books written here are still read. Michael's chronicle and Bar Hebraeus's histories remain primary sources for anyone who studies the medieval Middle East. Bar Hebraeus also wrote a book of church law and a grammar of Syriac. Scholars see this period as the last great flowering of Syriac writing before a long decline.
